desc:
You get unsorted closed intervals [start, end] and a tolerance gap. Two intervals are close when the empty space between them is at most gap: that is, when they overlap, or when the later one starts at most gap units after the earlier one ends. Closeness is chained: if A is close to B and B is close to C, all three end up in the same block, even if A and C are far apart.

Replace every block of connected intervals by the single interval from the smallest start to the largest end in the block. Return these merged intervals sorted by start.

intervals = [[1, 3], [6, 8], [2, 4], [20, 25], [11, 12]], gap = 3
result    = [[1, 12], [20, 25]]

Here [1,3] and [2,4] overlap, [6,8] starts 2 after 4, [11,12] starts 3 after 8, but [20,25] starts 8 after 12. With gap = 0 the task is the ordinary merge in which intervals sharing an endpoint are merged.
hints: Process the intervals in order of start, so that each new interval can only be close to the block that was built last.
To decide whether the new interval joins the last block, compare its start with the largest end in that block, not with the end of the previous interval.
Sort by start. If start - lastEnd ≤ gap extend lastEnd = max(lastEnd, end); otherwise open a new block.
editorial: This is the classic merge-intervals sweep with a different join condition. Sort by start. Keep the result list; for the next interval compare start - blockEnd with gap, where blockEnd is the right end of the last block (the maximum end of everything in it). If the distance is at most gap (negative or zero means overlap), the interval joins the block and blockEnd = max(blockEnd, end); otherwise it starts a new block.

Comparing against the block's maximum end is essential: an earlier long interval can still reach a late start even though the interval just before it ended early. After sorting, nothing later can reach back into a closed block, because starts only grow. Time O(n log n) for the sort, O(n) for the output.
